extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsel / PR practitioners and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations practitioners on forming, influencing, and measuring public opinion through press and other media, grounded in group and crowd psychology. Emphasizes strategies, media selection, timing, and the psychological foundations necessary for successful campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press reflects the people it serves
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers, like governments, fairly reflect the people they serve; an objectionable paper is often 'a trifle better than the patrons on whom it relies for its support.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility for journalistic evils must be divided between press and public; expect the press to mirror prevailing public attitudes and values rather than to operate independently. Use this as a constraint when setting expectations for press influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual interaction between press and public
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor 'listens for the echo of his words' — action and reaction continuously occur between the press and its patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat influence as bidirectional: the press shapes public opinion and is shaped by it. Strategies should account for feedback loops (public reaction modifies future media behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist established points of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of any force attempting to modify public opinion depends upon the success with which it is able to enlist established points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and work within existing attitudes, stereotypes, and group standards rather than expecting wholesale immediate conversion. 'Enlist' sympathetic authorities, institutions, or framings to gain acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple interacting media and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The press, schools, churches, motion pictures, advertising, lecture platform and radio all both conform to public demands and influence the public in turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns that coordinate across media and institutions (press, film, lectures, advertising, schools, religious bodies) to leverage mutual reinforcement and reach different facets of the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test and exploit public reaction (trial balloons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements were used by diplomats as 'a happy means of testing popular opinion upon the various projects offered in council.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled public disclosures or 'trial balloons' to gauge reaction and adjust strategy; monitor clippings and reactions daily to guide policy or campaign adjustments. Beware that publicity can materially alter events (e.g., diplomatic proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring the public into confidence to secure cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening proceedings to the press (Hague Conference) assured public cooperation and aided delegates in testing and shaping proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, provide transparency and proactive information to shape favorable public response and enlist cooperation; timely disclosure can create readiness to accept policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and timing of news determine perceived importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors 'winnow' the day's facts; 'All the news that a newspaper prints is affected by what else happened that day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for news cycles and competing events: timing determines placement and prominence. On busy news days, less sensational items are displaced. Plan releases to avoid being buried and to exploit slow news periods for greater impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance giving the public what it wants with giving it what it should want
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'very human tendency to compromise between giving the public what it wants and giving the public what it should want.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft messaging that is palatable to target audiences while nudging them toward desired norms—avoid messaging that is so far from expectations it will be rejected; meanwhile, consider occasions to 'brave the public' when leadership requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use purposeful campaigns combining appeals and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements like Safety First used every form of appeal—poster, circular, lecture, law enforcement, motion pictures, 'safety weeks'—to change habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a mix of persuasive communication (ads, films, lectures, posters) and practical measures (education, enforcement, events) for behavior-change campaigns. Multi-pronged approaches are more likely to produce durable change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analysis, investigation and applied expertise with public education
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rockefeller Foundation attacked hookworm by analysis, investigation, applied medical principles, and public education to change habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine technical/analytical credibility (research, expert endorsement) with educational outreach to win acceptance for technical or health-related interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study 'mirrors' of the public mind to reveal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of the mirrors of the public mind — the press, the motion pictures, the lecture platform — reveals what their standards are and those of the groups they reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct media and audience analysis to understand the standards, tastes, and expectations of different group segments; use this intelligence to tailor messages and select channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand individual and group psychology as groundwork
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental study of group and individual psychology is required before the public relations counsel can determine how readily individuals or groups will accept modifications of viewpoints or policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in psychological and sociological study (stereotypes, crowd/herd behavior, motivations) to predict receptivity, design interventions, and choose persuasive tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage stereotypes and pre-existing definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological 'stereotypes' are shorthand that 'largely determine what group of facts we shall see and in what light we shall see them.' 'We define first and then see.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame messages to align with or gradually shift prevailing stereotypes; recognize that audiences often perceive facts through pre-existing cultural patterns—work with those patterns rather than ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize herd/crowd mechanisms and their five tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'herd' (gregarious tendency) produces homogeneity and five characteristics: intolerance of solitude; greater sensitivity to the voice of the herd; susceptibility to pack/herd passions (mob/panic); remarkable susceptibility to leadership; and relations dependent on recognition as a herd member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design appeals that acknowledge herd instincts: provide recognizable group cues, authoritative leaders or symbols, and foster a sense of belonging. Beware of unintended mob dynamics and moral hazards when activating herd sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for contextual influences (precedent, authority, habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: No idea or opinion is isolated; it is surrounded and influenced by precedent, authority, habit and other human motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map contextual anchors (authorities, historical precedents, habitual behaviors) before campaigning; strategies that ignore these will likely fail or be resisted. Use respected authorities and habit-shaping tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigns may need editorial courage or restraint depending on morale goals
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper 'has a hard and fast duty to perform in keeping up the morale of the community' yet also sometimes must 'brave their public' when leading is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide strategically whether the objective is to sustain morale (favoring constructive emphasis) or to challenge public views (requiring sustained editorial courage); measure risk of backlash versus long-term benefits.
